opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. For me the starting point was a fairly simple observation: a standard transformer spends a fixed amount of compute on every token, no matter how easy or hard the problem is. The model has a set number of layers, and that's its budget. If you want it to "think harder," the main lever people use today is to have it write out more tokens, a chain of thought, and do the reasoning in language.

That works, but it always struck me as a little odd as the only option. Language is a lossy, discretized bottleneck. Every time the model commits to a token, it throws away a lot of what was in its internal state. There's a lot of reasoning that probably isn't naturally verbalizable. You'd like the model to be able to reason in its continuous latent space, and to spend more compute there when it needs it.

Recurrent depth is a very direct way to get that. Instead of a stack of unique layers, you have a block of layers that you apply repeatedly. You loop it. At training time you randomize the number of iterations, so the model learns to use however much depth it's given. Then at test time you can just turn up the number of recurrences on a hard problem and the model gets to compute longer, without producing any extra tokens and without needing specialized chain-of-thought training data.

There's also a bit of history behind it for me. Before language models, we'd done work on recurrent networks for things like algorithmic reasoning and puzzles, where you could train on small problems with a few iterations and then, by running more iterations at test time, solve much larger instances than you ever trained on. That extrapolation behavior was really striking. So the question was a natural one: does this still work at the scale of a real language model, and do you get that same kind of test-time scaling in reasoning? That's what pushed us to actually train a model of a few billion parameters this way and find out.

And beyond performance, it's just a scientifically interesting object. You get some nice properties almost for free, like adaptive compute per token, where the model can exit early on easy tokens, and you can look at the trajectories of the latent state as it iterates and see what kinds of structure show up in how the model is "thinking." So it's a direction that's both practically useful and gives you a new lens on what these models do internally.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. So the way I came to it was really through thinking about what test-time compute means. Everyone's seen the chain-of-thought results, where you let a model generate more tokens and it gets better at reasoning tasks. But if you step back, that's a somewhat strange way to spend compute. You're forcing the model to externalize every intermediate step into a discrete token, and then you're spending a full forward pass on each of those tokens. A lot of what the model might want to "think about" doesn't naturally have a verbal form. Spatial reasoning, arithmetic, keeping track of structure in a problem — those aren't obviously things that want to be written down in English.

So the question we asked was: what if the model could just think in its latent space instead? Recurrent depth is a very old idea in some sense. You take a block of transformer layers and you just apply it repeatedly, feeding the hidden state back into itself. The model can iterate as many times as it needs on a given input before it commits to a token. It's closer to how you'd design a system where the amount of computation is proportional to the difficulty of the problem, rather than fixed by the architecture.

There were a few things that made it appealing to me specifically. One is scaling. The models we're all training now get their capability largely by adding parameters, and that's expensive in memory, in training infrastructure, in deployment. Recurrence lets you scale compute without scaling parameters. A relatively small model can, in principle, behave like a much deeper one at inference time, and you decide per-query how deep to go.

The second thing is that it's compute that doesn't need specialized training data. Chain-of-thought works really well when you have lots of examples of reasoning traces, or when you can do reinforcement learning on verifiable problems. Recurrent depth you can train on ordinary pretraining data, because the recurrence is just part of the forward pass. The model learns to use it the same way it learns to use its layers.

And then honestly, the third thing is that it's a bit contrarian. There's been a lot of folklore that recurrent architectures are hard to train at scale, that they're unstable, that transformers won precisely because they're not recurrent. We wanted to know whether that was actually true, or whether people just stopped trying around 2017. The answer, as far as we can tell, is that with some care in how you inject the input at each step and how you randomize the number of iterations during training, you can train these things at reasonable scale, and they do pick up interesting behavior. The model learns to spin up a kind of computation in latent space that you can actually look at and, in some cases, interpret.

r001.rationale: The response says recurrent depth lets a model do more computation on a problem before producing a token, and describes latent-space thinking as useful for reasoning tasks.

r002.rationale: The response does not mention mixture-of-experts models or their parameter capacity as a way to store information.

r003.rationale: It contrasts recurrence with scaling parameters generally, but does not compare recurrent parameter reuse with sparse use of a larger mixture-of-experts parameter pool.

r004.rationale: It explicitly says the model can think in its latent space and repeatedly feeds the hidden state back through a transformer block.

astra-6.text:
What interested me was the idea that the amount of computation a language model uses could depend on how difficult the problem is. In a standard transformer, every token goes through a fixed number of layers. You’re spending roughly the same computation whether you’re completing a simple phrase or working through something that requires several steps of reasoning.

Recurrent depth gives you a way to revisit that. You take a block of the model and apply it repeatedly, letting it update its internal representation each time. So you can potentially spend more computation on a problem without adding more parameters, and without having to express every intermediate step as a token.

The interesting research question is whether the model learns to use those repetitions productively. Does it actually refine something, and can giving it more iterations lead to a better answer? That possibility of doing more work in the hidden state is what makes the approach compelling to me.

r002.rationale: It does not mention mixture-of-experts models or their parameter capacity.

r003.rationale: It describes reusing a block repeatedly but does not compare that with sparse use of a larger mixture-of-experts parameter pool.

r004.rationale: It identifies the internal representation, also called the hidden state, as where repeated computation occurs.

sol-6.1.text:
What interested me was the idea that a language model could spend more computation on a problem without needing more parameters. In a standard transformer, you go through a fixed stack of layers, so every token gets roughly the same amount of computation, whether you’re completing a simple phrase or working through something difficult.

With recurrent depth, you reuse a block of layers and let the hidden state evolve over multiple iterations. That gives you a way to ask: Can the model refine its computation internally? Can running it for longer actually help it arrive at a better answer?

And I found that particularly interesting as an alternative to doing all of that through generated text. Writing out a chain of thought is one way to spend more computation, but it’s not obvious that every intermediate step needs to be expressed in words. Recurrent depth gives us a way to explore computation in the model’s latent space.
